title: Opinions and attitudes
subtitle: Yes / No / Not Given and summary completion
summary: Read an argumentative text for the writer's tone, decide whether a statement matches the writer's views, and complete a summary with or without a box of answers.

lesson.heading: Adjectives carry the writer's attitude
lesson.text: The most difficult texts are in Reading Section 3. They argue for or against an idea, or set several arguments side by side. A writer's choice of words - above all their adjectives - shows how they feel about the topic.

examples.text: **Positive:** diverse, unspoilt, accomplished, productive, realistic, sophisticated, efficient, thorough, influential, prominent
**Negative:** disastrous, biased, vulnerable, dated, confusing, irrelevant, harsh, catastrophic, monotonous, distorted

lesson.note: In one passage about Lafayette Park the writer uses *world-class*, *renowned*, *great*, *beautiful* alongside *austere*, *unappealing* and *cavernous* - praise and reservation in the same breath.

lesson.heading: A view or a claim?

left.label: A claim
left.text: A statement the writer presents as **fact**.
examples: *Like hundreds of developments nationwide, they were the result of post-war urban renewal.*
*While much of Detroit began a steep decline soon after, Lafayette Park stayed afloat.*

right.label: A view
examples: *Detroit has an abundance of beautiful housing options.*
*There is a kind of austere uniformity to the townhouses when viewed from the outside.*
*Indeed, the best design doesn't force a personality on its residents.*

lesson.note: Yes / No / Not Given questions ask you to interpret the writer's views and claims. True / False / Not Given questions are about factual information. That is the only real difference between them.

lesson.heading: How to answer Yes / No / Not Given
rows: the statement agrees with the views or claims in the passage
the statement contradicts the views of the writer
it is impossible to say what the writer thinks
lesson.note: Check yourself: if you wrote YES, find the supporting line. If NO, correct the statement so it matches the writer. If NOT GIVEN, say what the passage **does** tell you instead.

lesson.heading: Worked examples
lesson.text: Each of these hangs on one detail. Read the statement twice before you go back to the passage.

examples.text: *It is the era in which Lafayette Park was developed that makes it special.* - **NO**
examples.note: Hundreds were built then; the writer says it was the three famous designers that made it unique.

examples.text: *Since 1962, many people have moved away from Detroit.* - **YES**
*Mies van der Rohe's designs influenced other architects in Detroit.* - **NOT GIVEN**
examples.note: We are only told that Mies designed Lafayette Park.

examples.text: *The exterior of each building has a distinct style.* - **NO**
examples.note: The buildings have *a kind of austere uniformity*.

examples.text: *Good architecture allows its occupants to reveal their identity.* - **YES**
examples.note: *The best design doesn't force a personality on its residents. Instead, it helps them bring out their own.*

lesson.heading: Summary completion, with and without a box
lesson.text: A **summary** is not a set of notes: it is complete sentences connected grammatically. So decide what **type** of word each gap needs - noun, verb, adjective, adverb - before you look for the answer. With a box, the options may be the passage's words or synonyms of them; without one, you must copy words from the text.

examples.text: *Lafayette Park was originally quite a ___ area of Detroit.*
examples.note: an adjective - **poor** (*land previously occupied by a working-class neighbourhood*)

examples.text: *its residents are more ___ than those in other areas*
examples.note: an adjective - **settled** (*one of the most racially integrated neighbourhoods ... economically stable*)

examples.text: *the residents feel quite ___ about the famous architecture*
examples.note: an adjective or adverb - **neutral** (*the casual attitude many residents have*)

examples.text: *they can ___ the townhouses and make them their own*

lesson.note: Use the **title** of the summary to find the part of the passage you need to read in detail.

lesson.text: A hyphenated word such as *long-term* counts as **one word**, and a number written in words such as *3.5 million* counts as a number. And you must use the words in the text: writing *fortnight* where the passage says *two weeks* is marked wrong.

exercises.prompt: Does each adjective suggest a positive or a negative tone?
What is the difference between True / False / Not Given and Yes / No / Not Given questions?
options: There is none - the words are interchangeable
True / False / Not Given is about factual information; Yes / No / Not Given is about the writer's views
Yes / No / Not Given questions never have a Not Given answer
True / False / Not Given questions appear only in General Training
exercises.explanation: The task is the same shape; what changes is whether you are judging facts or opinions.

exercises.prompt: The passage says hundreds of such developments were built then, but Lafayette Park was unique because of its three famous designers. Judge each statement.

items.text: The designers were unusually well known.
Many similar developments were built at that time.
It is the era Lafayette Park was built in that makes it special.
Lafayette Park was the only development of its kind.
The designers had worked together before.
The residents chose the designers themselves.

exercises.prompt: *In general, the residents feel quite ___ about the famous architecture they live in.* The passage says the writer was struck by the *casual attitude* many residents have.
exercises.explanation: Decide the gap needs an adjective first - that alone removes most of the options in the box.

exercises.statement: In a summary completion task without a box, you may replace a phrase from the passage with a shorter word of your own.
exercises.explanation: You must use the words in the text. Writing *fortnight* where the passage says *two weeks* is marked wrong.

exercises.prompt: Match each gap with the type of word it needs - and, where two gaps take the same part of speech, with the word itself.

pairs.left: different meerkat groups ___ at different times of day
young males were more ___ at problem solving
it was the ___ part of the container

exercises.prompt: The passage says only that Mies van der Rohe designed Lafayette Park. The statement is *Mies van der Rohe's designs influenced other architects in Detroit.*
exercises.explanation: No influence on others is mentioned either way, so it is impossible to say what the writer thinks.

exercises.statement: A hyphenated word such as *long-term* counts as one word for the purposes of a word limit.
exercises.explanation: And a number written in words, such as *3.5 million*, still counts as a number rather than as two words.

exercises.prompt: *A recent study discovered that young, male meerkats were more ___ than other members of their group at problem solving.* (ONE WORD ONLY)
exercises.explanation: The passage says *the more subordinate juvenile members of meerkat troops are the most innovative*.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that gives the writer's view of good design.
exercises.answer: The best design doesn't force a personality on its residents.
exercises.explanation: *The best ...* is an opinion presented as a principle - a view, not a claim of fact.
